title: SimpleX: messaging and application platform
note: Overview of SimpleX: no user identifiers, unidirectional per-contact queues on relays, 2-hop onion private routing. Hides: relationship from servers (separate queues per contact, no global ID), content (E2EE), sender IP from recipient's relay (private routing). Does not hide: timing and queue activity from a colluding relay pair; recipient IP from its own relay.
bitmessage_link: Replaces Bitmessage's flood-and-trial-decrypt recipient ambiguity with unlinkable per-contact queues addressed by random IDs; no global broadcast so bandwidth is O(own messages), at the cost of trusting that sender and recipient relays do not collude.

title: SimpleX Messaging Protocol (SMP)
note: Spec of SMP: recipient-created unidirectional simplex queues with separate sender/recipient IDs and keys, per-queue command auth, deniable client authentication, queue rotation, proxying. Hides: sender identity and sender-recipient link from the server (different IDs per direction), content. Leaks: message timing and sizes (padded), recipient IP to its own server.
bitmessage_link: Server-held queue with receiver-chosen random addresses is the opposite design to Bitmessage's broadcast stream; admission control is by authenticated queue commands rather than proof-of-work.

title: SimpleX Agent Protocol
note: Agent layer above SMP: duplex connections built from two simplex queues, X3DH-like handshake, double ratchet per connection, queue rotation to different servers. Hides: content, relationship from any single server; offers forward secrecy and post-compromise security per connection.
bitmessage_link: Gives each contact pair a ratcheted session with fresh queues, replacing Bitmessage's static-key per-address encryption with no forward secrecy.

title: Post-quantum resistant augmented double ratchet algorithm (PQDR)
note: Augments Signal double ratchet with encrypted headers and a hybrid Curve448+sntrup761 KEM in each ratchet step; compares with Signal PQXDH and Tutanota hybrid approaches. Content-only property (PQ forward secrecy and PCS); metadata unaffected.
bitmessage_link: Direct answer to Bitmessage's lack of any ratchet; adds PQ-hybrid session security to a metadata-private queue system.

title: SimpleX File Transfer Protocol (XFTP)
note: Large file transfer by splitting into encrypted chunks stored on independent relays, retrieved with one-time descriptions sent in-band. Hides: file content, link between chunks (different servers, per-chunk keys). Leaks chunk sizes.
bitmessage_link: Out-of-band bulk transfer avoids flooding large objects to every node as Bitmessage must.

title: SimpleX Remote Control Protocol (XRCP)
note: Protocol for a desktop to control a mobile app via authenticated, encrypted local channel with hybrid PQ KEM. Device-to-device; no network metadata concerns.
bitmessage_link: none direct (multi-device handling absent in Bitmessage)

title: SimpleX security and threat model
note: Threat model for SimpleX: what a single relay, colluding relays, a network observer and a compromised device can learn. States residual leaks: traffic correlation by global observer, IP exposure to own relay unless Tor, timing.
bitmessage_link: Explicit adversary matrix; Bitmessage has none and its flooding model hides recipient only against non-global observers.

title: SimpleX Push Notifications
note: Design of push notification delivery through APNS via notification server holding a per-queue token, without learning contacts or content. Leaks to Apple/notification server: device token and notification timing.
bitmessage_link: Mobile wake-up without polling a flood; Bitmessage has no mobile or push story.

title: SimpleX Chat Protocol
note: Application message format for direct and group chat on top of SMP/agent: groups are client-side meshes of pairwise connections, no server group state. Hides: group membership from servers.
bitmessage_link: Groups without Bitmessage-style chans: membership is decentralised in clients, not shared by a passphrase.

title: SimpleX Channels Protocol
note: Protocol for one-to-many channels via chat relays, so subscribers and owners stay unlinked from relay operators' view; roles for owners, relays and subscribers.
bitmessage_link: Channels are the closest SimpleX analogue to Bitmessage chans/broadcast, with relay trust instead of flooding.

title: SimpleX Channels: overview and design
note: Design rationale for decentralised channels: owner-signed content, redundant relays, subscriber privacy. Hides subscriber identity from relays and other subscribers; owner is known.
bitmessage_link: Publish/subscribe to a named feed without every node ingesting everything (contrast Bitmessage broadcasts).

title: SimpleX Chat Security Assessment (Trail of Bits, 2022-11-03)
note: One person-week review (Oct 2022) of SimpleX Chat: four findings (X3DH secrets not passed through HKDF, incorrect pad/unpad for long/short messages, key material in unpinned memory). Implementation and cryptography audit, not an analysis of the metadata claims.
bitmessage_link: Contrast: Bitmessage has no commissioned audit; this is the model for audited protocols in this wave.

title: SimpleX Chat Design Review: summary report (Trail of Bits, 2024-08-12)
venue: Trail of Bits design review summary, 2024-08
note: Design review of SMP, private routing and XRCP: protocols are only informally specified; a user-correlating side channel via the GET command; a compromised transport protocol enables more efficient correlation attacks; user correlation by introduced latency; XRCP lacks PFS and break-in recovery within sessions. Metadata-relevant findings about correlating users across queues.
bitmessage_link: Reviews the PQ ratchet and 2-hop routing that supersede Bitmessage-style static-key and flooding designs.

title: Session: End-To-End Encrypted Conversations With Minimal Metadata Leakage
venue: arXiv:2002.04609 (v1 Feb 2020, v3 Jul 2024); Session whitepaper
note: Session whitepaper: public-key IDs, swarms of staked Service Nodes store messages for 14 days, onion requests (3 hops) hide client IP. Hides: IP/network origin from storage nodes, content (E2EE); no phone number. Does not hide: recipient account ID from its swarm (swarm sees messages addressed to it), timing, and v1 dropped forward secrecy.
bitmessage_link: Recipient-addressed store-and-fetch in a small swarm replaces Bitmessage's flood to all nodes; Sybil cost is staking instead of per-message proof-of-work; sender anonymity via onion routing instead of broadcast mixing.

title: Oxen Session Audit: Technical Report (20-08-Oxen-REP v1.4)
note: Quarkslab audit (3 x 10 days: Android, iOS, Desktop, plus 10 days on the redesigned message encryption/signature protocol). Findings include no TLS verification when fetching node IPs and keys from seed nodes (high), and some requests not routed through the onion network, enabling ISP tracking (moderate). Not exhaustive; reviews app and onion-routing integration, not a proof of metadata privacy.
bitmessage_link: Independent review of an onion-routed, decentralised-storage design that replaces Bitmessage's flood model.

title: Session: Secure Messenger with additional Measures for Metadata Protection
venue: Seminar paper, Network Architectures and Services, TU Munich (NET-2020-11-1)
note: Academic-style secondary analysis of Session: public-key identifiers, decentralised network, onion routing; compares metadata protections with other messengers. Secondary source, not an independent audit.
bitmessage_link: Describes how Session replaces Bitmessage-like broadcast with onion routing plus swarm storage.

title: Session Protocol V2: PFS, Post-Quantum and the Future of Private Messaging
note: Proposed V2: per-device and per-account rotating keys for forward secrecy, ML-KEM post-quantum KEM, authorised device management. States V1 weaknesses: single long-term key, no forward secrecy after Signal protocol was dropped, harvest-now-decrypt-later, nodes that retain messages past the 14-day TTL. Content and session properties only; routing metadata unchanged.
bitmessage_link: Concrete statement that static long-term-key encryption (as in Bitmessage) lacks forward secrecy, and that ratchets are hard in decentralised multi-device storage.

title: Low Latency Anonymous Routing Protocol (LLARP) design
note: Design rationale for LLARP, a Tor/I2P hybrid onion router run by staked Service Nodes with a blockchain-fed DHT in place of directory authorities. Hides client IP from destination and route from relays; global-observer correlation not addressed.
bitmessage_link: Staked-node Sybil resistance as an alternative to Bitmessage's proof-of-work; network-layer source anonymity.

title: Cwtch: Privacy Preserving Infrastructure for Asynchronous, Decentralized, Multi-Party and Metadata Resistant Applications
note: Extends Ricochet with offline delivery and groups via untrusted, discardable Cwtch servers that relay group messages over Tor v3 onion services. Hides: IP of each party (Tor), content (E2EE), contact relationships from servers (servers see only group traffic; every member fetches all group messages). Leaks: group membership is not hidden from servers; all group members download all group messages (flood within group).
bitmessage_link: Closest analogue to Bitmessage chans: group fetch of all group messages from an untrusted server, but scoped to a small group and routed over Tor, not network-wide.

title: Bramble Synchronisation Protocol (BSP), version 0
note: Application-layer sync protocol for delay-tolerant networks: groups with message graphs, per-contact sync of offers/requests, no servers. Hides: content, and relationship to non-peers (no central index); but peers learn group membership. Metadata-hiding relies on Tor/transport.
bitmessage_link: Peer sync of per-group message sets replaces Bitmessage's global inventory exchange; no pow, only contact-authenticated peers.

title: Bramble Transport Protocol (BTP), version 4
note: Transport security with time-based key rotation, forward secrecy, padding and tags that conceal stream identity and let peers recognise the stream without identifiers. Hides content and stream link from non-contacts.
bitmessage_link: Forward secrecy and recognition tags by time-period key derivation, in contrast to Bitmessage's static address keys and trial decryption.

title: Bramble QR Code Protocol (BQP), version 4
note: In-person key agreement via QR commitments; produces shared secret not known to any other party. Hides: contact relationship from network observers until first contact.
bitmessage_link: Out-of-band key exchange avoids Bitmessage's public-address directory problem.

title: Bramble Handshake Protocol (BHP), version 0.1
note: Key agreement for delay-tolerant networks between peers who exchanged long-term public keys, producing ephemeral shared secret to upgrade BTP; handshake mode itself lacks forward secrecy.
bitmessage_link: Adds an ephemeral-key upgrade to a static-key bootstrap, one step beyond Bitmessage's fixed keys.

title: Bramble Rendezvous Protocol (BRP), version 0
note: Peers derive pseudo-random contact points (e.g. onion addresses) from shared keys, so no addresses need exchanging in advance. Hides: which pair is connecting, from outsiders without the shared key.
bitmessage_link: Derived rendezvous points replace trial-decrypting a global broadcast to find one's messages.

title: Pentest-Report Briar Project App & Protocol 03.2017
note: Cure53 pentest of Briar Android app plus review of BQP/BSP/BTP; twelve issues (e.g. DNS leak via RSS import, high severity), crypto review found no protocol break. Application-level metadata leak (DNS) noted.
bitmessage_link: Third-party review of a serverless, Tor/Bluetooth messenger; contrasts with Bitmessage's absence of audits.

title: Practically-exploitable Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Matrix
note: Several practically-exploitable attacks by a malicious homeserver on Matrix and Element end-to-end encryption, invalidating its confidentiality and authentication claims (insecure-by-design pieces, protocol confusion, missing domain separation, implementation bugs across Olm, Megolm, key backup, key sharing and verification). The server sees room membership, senders, timing and sizes by design.
bitmessage_link: Shows that federated-server mediation of group key distribution is a weaker trust base than Bitmessage's passphrase chans, but with server-visible metadata that Bitmessage's flood avoids.

title: Device-Oriented Group Messaging: A Formal Cryptographic Analysis of Matrix' Core
note: First formal model of Matrix group messaging (Device-Oriented Group Messaging): Matrix achieves confidentiality and authentication provided it introduces authenticated group membership; its state-sharing features (history sharing, account recovery) conflict with forward secrecy and post-compromise security. Content/session analysis; metadata out of scope.
bitmessage_link: Formal limits for symmetric sender-key group ratchets, relevant to Bitmessage chans which have no ratchet at all.

title: The Matrix Reloaded: A Mechanized Formal Analysis of the Matrix Cryptographic Suite
note: ProVerif symbolic models of Olm, Megolm and their composition (and of Sender Keys and Signal+Sender Keys): proves authentication, confidentiality, forward secrecy and PCS where they hold and mechanises known limitations and attacks. Content/session security only.
bitmessage_link: Mechanised-proof baseline for deployed group messaging; no counterpart exists for Bitmessage.

title: Olm Cryptographic Review
note: Targeted review of libolm 1.3.0 double ratchet and Megolm group ratchet: one high, one medium, six low, one informational finding, including unknown-key-share attacks. Content security only.
bitmessage_link: Review of the double-ratchet and group-ratchet constructions that Bitmessage lacks.

title: Olm: A Cryptographic Ratchet (specification)
note: Matrix's implementation of the double ratchet with Curve25519 one-time keys for 1:1 sessions. Content only; Matrix server sees who talks to whom.
bitmessage_link: Ratcheted pairwise sessions in contrast to Bitmessage's static address keys.

title: Megolm group ratchet (specification)
note: Per-sender hash ratchet for group messages; room members share session keys via Olm. Weak PCS and forward secrecy only for ratcheted-forward state; later joiners can be given earlier keys.
bitmessage_link: A sender-key group scheme: the middle ground between Bitmessage chan passphrases and full tree-based group key agreement.

title: Matrix Server-Server (Federation) API specification
note: Federation protocol: every homeserver in a room replicates a signed event DAG; servers see room membership, sender identities, timestamps and event sizes. Hides content only via separate E2EE; hides nothing about relationships from participating servers.
bitmessage_link: Federated full replication of room history among servers, vs Bitmessage's network-wide flood; membership and metadata are server-visible.

title: A Glimpse of the Matrix (Extended Version): Scalability Issues of a New Message-Oriented Data Synchronization Middleware
note: Analyses the Matrix federation protocol as replicated data sync and measures scalability bottlenecks (state resolution, event replication to all servers in a room). Not a privacy analysis.
bitmessage_link: Cost of full-replication-per-room, a bounded analogue of Bitmessage's flood-to-everyone bandwidth.

title: MSC1442: State Resolution: Reloaded
note: Proposal defining state resolution v2 for Matrix rooms, aimed at mitigating known state-reset attacks in a federated event DAG.
bitmessage_link: none direct (consistency in federated rooms; Bitmessage has no ordering or access control)

title: MSC4297: State Resolution v2.1
note: Modifies state resolution to reduce 'state resets' (access-control failures in a decentralised event DAG), room version 11 base.
bitmessage_link: none direct (federated access control)

title: MSC4268: Sharing room keys for past messages
note: Lets new room members receive keys for earlier messages. Weakens forward-secrecy in exchange for usability; metadata is unchanged.
bitmessage_link: Joiner-gets-history is the normal case in Bitmessage chans (anyone with the passphrase reads everything); Matrix makes it an explicit policy.

title: MSC1756: Cross-signing devices with device signing keys
note: Cross-signing hierarchy so users verify one identity rather than each device key; central to the key-verification attacks in Albrecht et al.
bitmessage_link: Multi-device authentication that Bitmessage (one key per address) does not address.

title: Ricochet Security Assessment (public report)
venue: NCC Group / Open Technology Fund report, 2016-02-15
note: Audit of Ricochet (Tor v2 onion-service peer-to-peer messenger with no servers): found one deanonymisation issue (fixed in 1.1.2) and several hardening items. Ricochet hides: IP of both parties (Tor), content, and social graph from servers (none exist); both must be online to deliver.
bitmessage_link: Direct sender-recipient channel over Tor onion services; no flood, no offline delivery, no group support.

title: Cwtch Security Handbook: Risk Model
note: Threat model naming the communication contexts Cwtch tries to protect (who, where, when, what, how) and the adversaries considered; metadata-resistance framing. Cwtch hides: IPs (Tor), who talks to whom outside the group/server; leaks that servers see group traffic volume and timing.
bitmessage_link: Explicit metadata context list, in the style that Bitmessage lacks.

title: Cwtch Security Handbook: Cwtch Server
note: Describes the untrusted Cwtch server that stores and fans out group messages to all connected members; servers can be discarded. Server sees group message volume and online peers' onion identities, not content.
bitmessage_link: Server-held group stream every member fetches in full, as in a Bitmessage stream scoped to a small group.

title: Cwtch Security Handbook (introduction)
note: Entry page of the Cwtch secure-development handbook; points to Tapir, Cwtch, group and server components.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: The Tox Protocol Specification (TokTok)
note: Tox's DHT-based peer discovery, onion paths for announcing and finding long-term keys, and crypto using NaCl; no ratchet in the legacy protocol (static keys with session nonces). Hides: friend key lookups from DHT nodes via onion paths. Leaks IP address to friends and DHT neighbours; no offline messages.
bitmessage_link: Direct peer connections with a DHT, instead of a flood. The legacy design lacks forward secrecy like Bitmessage.

title: Wesh Protocol (Berty)
note: Offline-first messaging over IPFS/libp2p (DHT, PubSub, OrbitDB logs) with BLE and mDNS local transports; groups for multi-device, contacts and multi-member chats. Peers meet at rendezvous points derived from shared secrets. No central directory, so metadata collection is minimised, but the spec itself states IPFS is not privacy-focused: any peer can resolve a peerID to its public IP, and anonymising transports (Tor) are only planned.
bitmessage_link: Shared-secret-derived rendezvous points replace Bitmessage's flood for finding one's messages; no source anonymity unless a mixing transport is added.

title: The Internals of Veilid: A New Distributed Application Framework
note: Veilid design: DHT for private-route and value storage, safety routes (sender privacy) plus private routes (receiver privacy) composed so no node knows both ends. Hides sender and receiver network location from each other and from relays; no global-adversary claim.
bitmessage_link: Dual-route compose of sender and receiver privacy replaces Bitmessage's flood-for-recipient-ambiguity.

title: Scuttlebutt Protocol Guide
note: Append-only signed feeds replicated by gossip (EBT) along the follow graph; private messages via private-box to up to 7 recipients. Private-box hides content and recipient identities from non-recipients, but sender feed, timing and message size are public. Every follower trial-decrypts.
bitmessage_link: Closest deployed relative: recipients trial-decrypt public feed messages; flood replaced by follow-graph gossip; sender is public (no source anonymity).

title: Autocrypt Level 1 Specification, Release 1.1.0
venue: Autocrypt specification (Release 1.1.0 dated 2020-12-21; level-1 spec first released 2017)
note: Opportunistic OpenPGP key exchange in email headers, with key gossip for groups. Hides content only; email headers and mail servers reveal sender, recipient and timing.
bitmessage_link: E2EE over federated email, versus Bitmessage's own network; metadata fully visible to mail providers.

title: Cryptographic Analysis of Delta Chat
note: Attacks on Delta Chat's Autocrypt/SecureJoin/OpenPGP use: key-confusion, group membership and signature issues; Delta Chat inherits email-server metadata exposure. Analysis is of content authentication and group security, not metadata.
bitmessage_link: Shows weakness of email-based group E2EE without ratchets; no forward secrecy, like Bitmessage.

title: The PQXDH Key Agreement Protocol (revision 3)
note: Adds CRYSTALS-Kyber KEM to X3DH for post-quantum-protected initial key agreement; server-held prekey bundles. Content-only; Signal server knows account IDs and contact graph timing.
bitmessage_link: PQ session establishment that Bitmessage's static ECC keys lack.

title: The X3DH Key Agreement Protocol
note: Asynchronous key agreement from server-held prekeys; deniable. A server is required to hold prekeys and sees who fetches whose bundle.
bitmessage_link: Asynchronous initial key exchange against static addresses; Bitmessage has none.

title: The Double Ratchet Algorithm
note: Specification of the double ratchet giving forward secrecy and post-compromise security with out-of-order delivery.
bitmessage_link: The ratchet that Bitmessage lacks; static address keys give no forward secrecy.

title: Formal verification of the PQXDH Post-Quantum key agreement protocol for end-to-end secure messaging
note: ProVerif and CryptoVerif proofs of PQXDH including a KEM re-encapsulation attack that motivated spec changes. Content/session security only.
bitmessage_link: State of the art for verifying PQ session setup in a deployed messenger.

title: All the Numbers are US: Large-scale Abuse of Contact Discovery in Mobile Messengers
note: Measurement of contact-discovery abuse in WhatsApp, Signal and Telegram: mass crawls of phone numbers, profile data and OS/device leakage; proposes mitigations. Shows phone-number identifiers make the social graph enumerable regardless of E2EE.
bitmessage_link: Contrast: Bitmessage addresses are random keys, so no identifier-based enumeration, but also no discovery.

title: Poster: No safety in numbers: traffic analysis of sealed-sender groups in Signal
note: Extends the Martiny et al. statistical disclosure attack on Signal's sealed sender from pairs to whole group conversations: the server, seeing who receives messages and the receipts, can recover group membership. Sealed sender hides the sender per message only.
bitmessage_link: Concrete traffic-analysis limit on sender hiding without batching or cover traffic; Bitmessage's flood avoids recipient-side leakage but is global-adversary timing-exposed.

title: Careless Whisper: Exploiting Silent Delivery Receipts to Monitor Users on Mobile Instant Messengers
note: Silent delivery receipts triggered by crafted messages let any user who knows a phone number ping the target without notification, in WhatsApp and Signal: tracks the target across companion devices, infers daily schedule and activity, counts active sessions and OS, and drains battery or data. A metadata leak by design of receipts, independent of E2EE.
bitmessage_link: Delivery receipts are a metadata channel absent in Bitmessage (no ACKs), but trade off reliability.

title: WhatsApp Encryption Overview: Technical white paper
venue: WhatsApp technical white paper (Version 9, 2026-02-25; first edition 2016)
note: Describes WhatsApp's Signal-protocol E2EE, sender-key groups, multi-device, sealed-sender-like server blindness for some fields. WhatsApp servers know phone numbers, group membership sizes, timing; contents hidden.
bitmessage_link: Mainstream baseline against which Bitmessage-era designs are measured; central server with strong content security and weak metadata privacy.

title: Three Lessons From Threema: Analysis of a Secure Messenger
note: Cryptographic analysis of Threema's custom protocols (client-server, end-to-end, device-to-device) finding several attacks and weaknesses after a decade of deployment; lessons on proprietary protocols and weak composition. Content and authentication focus; the Threema server sees metadata.
bitmessage_link: Deployed custom-crypto messenger analysed after 10+ years; Bitmessage's ad-hoc design faces similar risks.

title: Breaking Bridgefy, again: Adopting libsignal is not enough
note: Attacks on Bridgefy's Bluetooth mesh messenger after it adopted libsignal: still allows user-impersonation, MITM and denial-of-service; shows library adoption not sufficient. Mesh broadcasts are visible to nearby nodes (sender and routing metadata exposed).
bitmessage_link: Mesh flooding of encrypted blobs, as in Bitmessage but over Bluetooth; analysed under protest-scale threat models.

title: XIP-49: Decentralized backend for MLS messages
note: Architecture for a decentralised XMTP: node-to-node and client-to-node protocols, permissioned node registry as NFTs, identity updates ordered on a blockchain, payers compensating node operators. Clients provide MLS E2EE; nodes see wallet-linked inbox IDs, group membership events, message sizes and timing. Hides only content.
bitmessage_link: MLS group security over a permissioned, paid broker mesh with on-chain ordering of identity/membership; opposite end of the spectrum from Bitmessage's anonymous flood.

title: XIP-46: Multi-wallet identity
note: Replaces wallet-address identity with Inbox IDs bound to multiple wallets and installations. Associations are public to the network: wallet-to-inbox links are not hidden.
bitmessage_link: Wallet identity makes the social graph linkable by chain address; contrast with Bitmessage's pseudonymous addresses.

title: XIP-42: Universal 'allow' and 'block' preferences
note: Client-side consent lists (allowed/denied addresses), stored as an encrypted message on a user-preferences topic, to filter spam in a wallet-addressed inbox. Spam control is by recipient-side allow-list rather than sender cost.
bitmessage_link: Recipient-side filtering as an alternative to Bitmessage's per-object proof-of-work.

title: Farcaster Specifications (version 2023.11.15)
note: On-chain id registry plus signed messages replicated among hubs via CRDT sync. All protocol messages (casts, reactions, follows) are public; the spec contains no private-message type, so direct casts sit outside it. Hides nothing about sender, topic or timing.
bitmessage_link: Public pub/sub-like feed replicated among hubs; useful as a non-private control for Bitmessage's private broadcast.

title: 10/WAKU2: Waku v2
note: Modular privacy-focused messaging protocol suite (relay, filter, lightpush, store) over libp2p GossipSub; content-topic subscription with pubsub-topic sharding. Hides: sender (StrictNoSign, no peer-id signing), content if encrypted; leaks IP to connected peers, topic interest to GossipSub neighbours. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Successor to Ethereum Whisper (Bitmessage-like flood with PoW) using GossipSub and RLN instead of PoW.

title: 11/WAKU2-RELAY
note: Specifies relay over GossipSub with StrictNoSign policy, so published messages carry no sender or seqno; recipients are hidden among all subscribers of the pubsub topic (k-anonymity by topic). Weak against traffic analysis at the network level. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Topic-level recipient ambiguity (k-anonymity) is a bandwidth-bounded version of Bitmessage's whole-stream flood; the flood cost scales with topic traffic instead of the whole network.

title: 14/WAKU2-MESSAGE
note: WakuMessage format: payload, content topic, version, timestamp, ephemeral flag, optional RLN proof; version determines payload encryption. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Message envelope akin to Bitmessage objects but carrying a rate-limiting proof rather than PoW.

title: 26/WAKU2-PAYLOAD
note: Payload encryption schemes for Waku messages: ECIES to a recipient public key or symmetric AES-GCM; optional signature. No forward secrecy at this layer. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Same static-key encryption model as Bitmessage's; higher layers (X3DH, Noise) add sessions.

title: 17/WAKU2-RLN-RELAY
note: Relay variant requiring a zk membership proof and RLN share per epoch, so exceeding the per-epoch rate reveals the sender's secret and enables slashing; senders stay anonymous within the membership set. Hides sender within group; membership registration is on-chain. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Direct replacement for Bitmessage's proof-of-work admission: rate limit enforced cryptographically with stake and slashing.

title: 54/WAKU2-X3DH-SESSIONS
note: X3DH-based session establishment over Waku with double ratchet; bundles published in a content topic. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Adds forward-secret sessions over a Bitmessage-like anonymous topic network.

title: Noise sessions in Waku for 1-to-1 communication
note: Noise handshake-based session setup for 1:1 channels over Waku content topics with deterministic topic derivation and optional QR pairing.
bitmessage_link: Derives rendezvous content topics from handshake secrets, similar in spirit to Briar's BRP and Bitmessage's tag-based lookup.

title: RLN-STEALTH-COMMITMENTS (RLN stealth commitment usage)
note: Uses stealth-address style commitments so RLN membership registrations are unlinkable to registering identities. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Reduces linkability of rate-limit credentials, relevant to anonymous admission replacing proof-of-work.

title: Midnight ledger specification: Zswap (shielded coin protocol)
note: Zswap: commitment/nullifier sets for shielded coins; output carries an optional ciphertext (DH over embedded curve, Poseidon-CTR) delivering the coin secret to the receiver. Hides amount, owner and sender-receiver link; the spec defines no messaging channel or event type, and ciphertext presence is optional (delivery may go offchain).
bitmessage_link: Same structure as Bitmessage for recipient discovery: outputs are public and recipients must scan; no tags.

title: Zcash Protocol Specification (Sprout, Overwinter, Sapling, Orchard)
note: Normative spec of shielded notes with 512-byte memo field inside the note ciphertext; every shielded output is public and recipients trial-decrypt. Hides: sender, recipient, amount, memo for shielded-to-shielded transfers. Public: existence and time of transaction, fee, pool value balance, ciphertext sizes. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: A ledger doing what Bitmessage does: global broadcast of ciphertexts, recipients trial-decrypt, with ledger-level spam cost (fees) instead of proof-of-work.

title: ZIP 302: Standardized Memo Field Format
note: Defines how the 512-byte memo carries UTF-8 text, binary, or empty content so wallets can use shielded transactions as an encrypted message channel. Content and the sender-recipient link are hidden; each message costs a transaction fee.
bitmessage_link: On-chain private messaging with ledger fees as anti-spam.

title: ZIP 307: Light Client Protocol for Payment Detection
note: Light wallets download compact blocks (note ciphertext prefix without memo) and trial-decrypt locally, so the proxy learns nothing about which outputs are the user's; memos are fetched only for matches. Leaks: IP/timing unless Tor, and that a full transaction was later fetched. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Explicit bandwidth-privacy trade-off of downloading everything and scanning, i.e. Bitmessage's recipient privacy model with compression.

title: ZIP 231: Memo Bundles
note: Draft to replace the fixed 512-byte memo with variable-length, separately-encrypted memo bundles so shielded transactions can carry larger messages without scanning cost for non-recipients.
bitmessage_link: Addresses the scan-cost vs message-size trade-off that Bitmessage also faces.

title: Penumbra protocol specification: addresses, detection keys, fuzzy message detection, memos and note ciphertexts
note: Shielded chain whose addresses carry a detection key; senders attach fuzzy-message-detection clues so a delegated detection server can filter transactions for a user with no false negatives and a user-chosen false-positive rate (a tunable precision/anonymity trade-off). Note ciphertexts and memos are encrypted; sender, recipient and amounts hidden on-chain. Leaks: a detection entity given several detection keys can link the user's diversified addresses, and detection precision must adapt to the global message rate.
bitmessage_link: Applies fuzzy message detection to ledger outputs; a middle path between full trial-decrypt (Bitmessage) and tags.

title: Namada specification: Multi-Asset Shielded Pool (MASP)
note: Sapling-derived multi-asset shielded pool; notes carry encrypted ciphertext and a 512-byte memo, outputs scanned by viewing keys. Hides sender, recipient, amount and asset type of shielded transfers; transparent bridge amounts public.
bitmessage_link: Same scan-everything recipient model as Zcash/Bitmessage; shows no messaging-specific change.

title: Aztec documentation: private events, note discovery (tagging) and offchain message delivery
note: Private events encrypted to recipients; logs carry tag = poseidon2(shared_secret, index) so recipients query a node by tag instead of trial-decrypting; secret from arbitrary, address-derived, or non-interactive/interactive handshake; modes: onchain constrained/unconstrained or offchain. Hides content, and (with tags) which log belongs to whom to anyone lacking the secret; an onchain handshake reveals that a handshake was made with the recipient; the node serving tags sees which tags a client queries.
bitmessage_link: Moves from Bitmessage-style trial decryption to per-pair rolling tags, trading recipient privacy against the node for scan cost.

title: BIP 47: Reusable Payment Codes for Hierarchical Deterministic Wallets
note: Receiver publishes a payment code; sender sends a one-time notification transaction containing a blinded sender code, then derives per-payment addresses by ECDH. Hides payment links from outsiders, but the notification transaction is a public on-chain message revealing a relationship to the recipient's notification address (and the sender's inputs).
bitmessage_link: On-chain message hiding relationship only from observers who do not know the notification address.

title: BIP 352: Silent Payments
note: Static receiver address; sender derives unique output script from input keys; the receiver scans all eligible transactions with its scan key (delegable to a scan-only server). No notification message. Hides relationship and recipient from observers; sender inputs are public.
bitmessage_link: Scan-all recipient model on a public ledger, with the scan key delegable for bandwidth.

title: ERC-5564: Stealth Addresses
note: Announcer contract emits an Announcement event (stealth address, ephemeral key, 1-byte view tag, free-form metadata) that recipients scan with a viewing key; the view tag cuts scan work. Hides recipient identity behind stealth address; funding source of the stealth address and the announcement itself are public and linkable by timing.
bitmessage_link: On-chain announcement log that every recipient scans, with a view-tag optimisation; the metadata field is a small public message channel.

title: CIP-20: Transaction message/comment metadata
note: Metadata label 674 carries a plain-text message with a transaction. Hides nothing: sender, recipient addresses, content and time are public.
bitmessage_link: Baseline of a public on-chain message channel; the opposite of Bitmessage's goals.

title: CIP-83: Encrypted Transaction Message/Comment Metadata
note: Symmetric encryption of the CIP-20 message under a shared passphrase (default value public in the spec). Hides content from non-holders of the passphrase; sender, recipient addresses and timing remain public; not a recipient-hiding design.
bitmessage_link: Passphrase-shared encrypted message resembles a Bitmessage chan secret, but on a transparent ledger.

title: Session network documentation: Onion requests and message routing; Swarms
note: Sender fetches the recipient's swarm mapping by Account ID, then sends the message through a 3-hop onion request to a random swarm node, which replicates it to the swarm; stored until expiry (two weeks default). Hides sender IP from the swarm; the swarm for an Account ID is public, so who is receiving (and the volume and timing) is visible to its swarm nodes. Onion requests are TCP-based and limited to small messages.
bitmessage_link: Swarm-addressed delivery trades Bitmessage's whole-network recipient ambiguity for a small, public set of nodes per recipient, plus onion hops for sender anonymity.

title: Technical design of Ricochet
venue: Ricochet design document (ricochet-im; maintained in Ricochet Refresh)
note: Messenger where each user is a Tor hidden service and ID is the onion address; no server, no contact list stored elsewhere. Hides: IP of both parties, content, social graph from third parties. Both must be online; contact requests reveal onion address to the target.
bitmessage_link: Direct anonymous channel to a rendezvous point, removing any need for flooding or recipient ambiguity, but without store-and-forward.

title: Ricochet Protocol v3 (Tor v3 onion services)
authors: Ricochet Refresh / Blueprint for Free Speech
note: Wire protocol over Tor connection: packet/channel layers, contact request, chat channels, proof-of-possession of onion key. Content and identities hidden from network; each side learns the other's onion address after acceptance.
bitmessage_link: Peer-to-peer over Tor; no admission control other than contact approval (versus Bitmessage's PoW).

title: The Sesame Algorithm: Session Management for Asynchronous Message Encryption
note: Session management across multiple devices and sessions per user for asynchronous messaging; server-mediated device lists.
bitmessage_link: Multi-device session state, absent in Bitmessage.

title: The ML-KEM Braid Protocol
note: Sparse continuous key agreement using incremental ML-KEM, adding PQ post-compromise security to the Signal ratchet (triple ratchet). Content/session security only.
bitmessage_link: Shows the bandwidth cost of continuous PQ key agreement, directly relevant to constraints in flood-style networks.

title: Privacy-Preserving Abuse Detection in Future Decentralised Online Social Networks
venue: Preprint, INRIA/GNUnet (undated; c. 2016-2017; workshop version not confirmed)
note: Supervised-learning abuse detection for decentralised, E2EE social networks, with privacy-preserving protocols to compute the classifier's features; not yet resilient to a strong adaptive adversary. Hides message content and parts of the graph from the detector.
bitmessage_link: Alternative to proof-of-work for spam handling in decentralised messaging.

title: Jami developer documentation: swarm conversations, Dynamic Routing Table (DRT), identifiers, connection manager and synchronization
note: Conversation as a signed Git-like Merkle DAG synchronised directly between members, with a DHT used for rendezvous and invitations and a DRT overlay among members. Hides content (TLS and per-account certificates); members learn each other's IP, DHT nodes see account-hash lookups and timing. Messages now need a live peer connection, not DHT storage.
bitmessage_link: Moves from DHT-stored messages (a global-ish store, like Bitmessage's flood in spirit) to member-only overlays, shrinking ambiguity but exposing IPs to members.

title: Secure Scuttlebutt: An Identity-Centric Protocol for Subjective and Decentralized Applications
note: Academic description of SSB: signed append-only feeds replicated by gossip over social ties, subjective views. Hides nothing about publishers; private messages (private-box) hide recipient set from non-recipients but each follower trial-decrypts. No open copy retrieved (ACM DL answered 403; not circumvented).
bitmessage_link: Closest published design to Bitmessage-style trial decryption with social-graph gossip instead of a global flood.

title: CADET: Confidential Ad-hoc Decentralized End-to-End Transport
note: GNUnet transport for confidential, authenticated end-to-end connections in restricted-route (friend-to-friend, ad-hoc) networks; basis of GNUnet's messenger service. PDF link on bib.gnunet.org answered 404 during collection. Hides content via end-to-end encryption; relays learn path and timing.
bitmessage_link: End-to-end tunnels over a DHT-routed overlay, in contrast to flooding.

title: A Censorship-Resistant, Privacy-Enhancing and Fully Decentralized Name System
note: GNUnet Name System: records stored in a DHT under keys derived from zone key and label, so DHT nodes cannot learn the name queried or the answer. Query privacy against DHT nodes; no global namespace.
bitmessage_link: Private lookup of per-pair rendezvous information without a flood.

title: Kachina: Foundations of Private Smart Contracts
venue: CSF 2021; IACR ePrint 2020/543 (catalogued in cluster H-iog)
note: Formal model underlying Midnight's private contract state; no messaging channel, included for completeness of the Midnight stack. Already downloaded by cluster H-iog under this slug.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Zswap: zk-SNARK Based Non-Interactive Multi-Asset Swaps
venue: PoPETs 2022; IACR ePrint 2022/1002 (catalogued in cluster H-iog)
note: Academic basis of Midnight's Zswap shielded notes; see 2024-midnight-zswap-spec for the ledger spec and its optional ciphertext delivery. Already downloaded by cluster H-iog under this slug.
bitmessage_link: Shielded notes with recipient scanning, no messaging channel.

title: Security Assessment of DeltaChat's RPGP and RustCrypto RSA Libraries (Open Tech Fund)
venue: Include Security / OTF report, 2019 (first Delta Chat security review)
note: Library-level audit of rPGP and RustCrypto RSA used by Delta Chat for OpenPGP; implementation flaws, not protocol metadata. Draft report as published.
bitmessage_link: none direct (implementation audit of an email-based messenger)

title: Security Assessment of Delta Chat's Primary Rust Libraries (Open Technology Fund)
venue: Include Security / OTF report, 2020 (second Delta Chat security review)
note: Audit of the Delta Chat core Rust libraries including Autocrypt and SecureJoin handling, found issues in message parsing and key handling. Content/implementation security; email server metadata untouched.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: Pentest-Report Delta Chat Mail-Server Template & Libraries 02.2023 (MER-01)
venue: Cure53 report MER-01, February 2023 (third Delta Chat audit)
note: Audit of the chatmail/mail-server template and networking libraries; eight issues including unencrypted SQLite storage. Concerns the server side where all Delta Chat metadata resides.
bitmessage_link: none direct

title: An Empirical Analysis of Anonymity in Zcash
note: Measurement of how Zcash's anonymity set is eroded in practice: most value moves through transparent addresses; heuristics link shielded deposits and withdrawals. Shows ledger-level hiding depends on user behaviour and on timing/value correlations at the shield/unshield boundary.
bitmessage_link: Empirical limit on public-ledger sender/recipient hiding; analogous to timing correlation of Bitmessage objects at ingress and egress.

title: EIP-627: Whisper Specification
note: Whisper wire protocol: messages flood between peers with a per-node PoW requirement and Bloom-filter topic filtering, with direct peer-to-peer (mail-server) packets for history. Hides: recipient (flooded; trial decrypt by topic/key); sender if unsigned; the Bloom filter leaks interest to neighbours. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Direct descendant of Bitmessage's design: flood, PoW admission, trial-decrypt, with Bloom-filter topic narrowing.

title: Mesh Messaging in Large-scale Protests: Breaking Bridgefy
note: Security analysis of Bridgefy (Bluetooth mesh messenger used in protests): users could be tracked, no authenticity, no effective confidentiality, resilience failures; an adversary can build social graphs, read and forge messages and shut down the network with one crafted message. Mesh broadcast leaks sender IDs and message metadata to anyone in radio range. [Duplicate: already catalogued and downloaded by cluster PB1 under this slug; the PB6 reading in this note is retained.]
bitmessage_link: Mesh/flood messaging in the field: Bitmessage-like broadcast without authenticated, anonymous design, with real-world consequences.

title: Analysis and Improvements of the Sender Keys Protocol for Group Messaging
venue: arXiv:2301.07045; Asiacrypt 2023 as 'WhatsUpp with Sender Keys?'
note: Formal analysis of Sender Keys (the group protocol in WhatsApp and Signal groups): shows lack of post-compromise security and proposes a more efficient variant with PCS; content/session analysis, metadata outside scope.
bitmessage_link: Limits of symmetric sender-key group schemes; Bitmessage chans correspond to a simpler no-ratchet shared-key group.

title: Triple Ratchet: A Bandwidth Efficient Hybrid-Secure Signal Protocol
note: Hybrid classical/PQ ratchet that adds a sparse KEM-based ratchet to the Signal double ratchet, cutting the bandwidth of PQ updates; the basis of Signal's deployed SPQR. Content/session security only.
bitmessage_link: Shows bandwidth cost for PQ continuous key agreement, relevant where each message must be flooded.

title: Anonymity Analysis of the Umbra Stealth Address Scheme on Ethereum
note: Four heuristics identify the real recipient of 48.5% (Ethereum), 25.8% (Polygon), 65.7% (Arbitrum), 52.6% (Optimism) of Umbra stealth payments, mostly via funding and withdrawal linking. Recipient hiding by stealth addresses fails in practice because of gas-funding and reuse patterns.
bitmessage_link: Empirical limit of announce-and-scan recipient privacy on a public ledger.

title: BaseSAP: Modular Stealth Address Protocol for Programmable Blockchains
note: Modular base-layer stealth address protocol (basis of ERC-5564) with announcements on a contract, dual-key secp256k1 scheme, cost analysis and attack vectors against recipient privacy. Hides recipient behind stealth address; announcement metadata and funding are public.
bitmessage_link: On-chain announcement and scan, closest ledger analogue to Bitmessage's tagged flood.

title: Four Attacks and a Proof for Telegram
note: Analysis of MTProto 2.0 symmetric cryptography: four attacks (one practical, one theoretical, one timing side channel in three official clients, chained with a key-exchange server attack that enables a MitM) and a proof for a slightly modified variant. Telegram cloud chats are not E2EE; the server sees content and metadata.
bitmessage_link: Reminder that mainstream messengers' default mode is client-server visible; strong metadata hiding is absent.

title: A Formal Security Analysis of the Signal Messaging Protocol
venue: IACR ePrint 2016/1013; EuroS&P 2017; J. Cryptology 2020 (extended version July 2019)
note: First provable-security analysis of Signal's multi-stage key exchange including double-ratchet state; proves key indistinguishability with forward secrecy and post-compromise security under compromise models. Content/session only.
bitmessage_link: Defines the session-security bar that Bitmessage's static-key encryption does not meet.

title: Improving Signal's Sealed Sender
note: Shows Signal's sealed sender (sender hidden from the server) does not compose over a conversation: statistical disclosure attacks, made effective by default delivery receipts, link sealed-sender users in as few as 5 messages (theory and simulation), even for users on Tor or VPN. Proposes provably secure mitigations at low cost. Sender hidden per message only; recipient, timing and reply pattern visible to the server.
bitmessage_link: Quantifies how weak sender hiding is without batching or cover traffic; Bitmessage hides recipients by flood but cannot hide sources to a global observer.

title: The Double Ratchet: Security Notions, Proofs, and Modularization for the Signal Protocol
note: Clean definition of secure messaging (forward security, post-compromise security, immediate decryption) and a modular generalised Signal protocol from continuous key agreement, forward-secure AEAD and a PRF-PRNG. Content/session security only.
bitmessage_link: Gives the formal target for session security that Bitmessage's static-key encryption does not reach, and the CKA primitive reused in PQ ratchets.

title: More is Less: On the End-to-End Security of Group Chats in Signal, WhatsApp, and Threema
note: Security model for dynamic-group messaging with delivery goals and a reverse-engineered description of the group protocols of Signal, WhatsApp and Threema; finds shortcomings such as a server (or an outsider) being able to add members or influence group state. Groups are pairwise fan-out; the server sees membership and timing.
bitmessage_link: Group membership integrity: Bitmessage chans have no membership at all (anyone with the passphrase is a member).

title: Measuring Freenet in the Wild: Censorship-Resilience under Observation
note: Passive and active measurement of the live Freenet network: size, churn, routing performance and robustness. Freenet stores content (not private messages); hides requester and publisher behind routing; the study shows what an observer learns about the topology. No open PDF located (publisher page only).
bitmessage_link: Freenet's darknet routing is a different answer to metadata hiding than flooding; useful as a measured baseline.

title: Dealing with Dead Ends: Efficient Routing in Darknets
note: Shows that greedy routing in friend-to-friend overlays such as Freenet's darknet mode has dead ends and proposes polylogarithmic routing with provable guarantees. Hides: topology beyond one's friends; routing metadata at each hop.
bitmessage_link: Provable routing cost in trust-graph overlays, an alternative to flooding with different scaling.

title: Private Communication Through a Network of Trusted Connections: The Dark Freenet
note: Design of the Freenet darknet mode: connections only between trusted friends, small-world routing, key-based storage. Pre-2012 background; kept only as the foundation of the Hyphanet line. No open copy located in this run.
bitmessage_link: Trust-graph routing as an alternative to Bitmessage's open flood.

title: Zerocash: Decentralized Anonymous Payments from Bitcoin (extended version)
note: Foundation of Zcash shielded notes: notes appear on chain as commitments with an encrypted payload for the recipient; spends reveal nullifiers; hides amounts and the sender-receiver link. Recipient discovery is by trial decryption of all new ciphertexts with the incoming viewing key. Transaction existence, time and fees public.
bitmessage_link: Ledger-wide broadcast with recipient trial-decrypt, the same recipient-ambiguity mechanism as Bitmessage, with the ledger's fee as admission cost.

title: Identity Leakage in Encrypted IM Call Services: An Empirical Study of Metadata Correlation
note: Passive ISP-level traffic correlation framework that links caller and callee flows in WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger and Snapchat calls using endpoint identifiability, shared server connectivity, call duration and volume symmetry, exposing social-graph edges without decryption. Shows E2EE does not hide who calls whom from a network observer. Open-access article; PDF not retrievable by the helper (publisher page returned no text), so metadata only.
bitmessage_link: Network-level relationship leakage of mainstream messengers, the problem that Bitmessage's flood and Tor-based designs aim to avoid.

title: Silent Exposure: A Comparative Study of Metadata Leakage in Encrypted Messaging Applications
note: Preprint comparing metadata leakage across WhatsApp, Messenger, Telegram, Signal, iMessage and Android Messages with a leakage taxonomy and score; Signal scores lowest. Evidence is based on a synthetic dataset (simulated presence logs and message interactions), so treat as low-evidence. SSRN preprint, not retrieved.
bitmessage_link: Comparative framing of what each messenger exposes (identity, presence, network, social graph); no direct Bitmessage content.

title: Why Can't I Just Use a Username? Understanding Why Users Struggle with Decentralized Messaging Apps
note: Title-level record: a user-facing study of why people struggle with decentralized messaging apps lacking usernames or phone numbers. Abstract not available from Crossref and no open PDF found, so contents unverified.
bitmessage_link: Usability cost of identifier-free addressing, the Bitmessage-address problem (long random addresses).

title: Practical Attacks on Session Messenger and Oxen Blockchain
note: Academic attacks on Session and the Oxen blockchain that supports its service-node network. Abstract unavailable from Crossref and no open copy retrieved (IEEE paywall, not circumvented); impact on Session's sender/recipient hiding therefore unverified here.
bitmessage_link: First peer-reviewed attack paper on the Session design that replaced Bitmessage-style flooding with staked swarms and onion requests.

title: The Signal Private Group System and Anonymous Credentials Supporting Efficient Verifiable Encryption
note: Group membership kept as encrypted entries on a central server; members authenticate with keyed-verification anonymous credentials, so group membership is visible to members but hidden from the service provider and outsiders. Hides group membership from the server; message delivery metadata still goes through the server.
bitmessage_link: Anonymous credentials for membership are the structured replacement for Bitmessage's shared-passphrase chans, with revocation and no server knowledge of the member list.

title: Parakeet: Practical Key Transparency for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging
note: Production-oriented key transparency (built around Meta's AKD used by WhatsApp): a privacy-preserving verifiable username-to-key map plus consistency protocol so a malicious server cannot silently serve false keys. Protects key authenticity (content security); the server still sees lookups and the contact graph by timing.
bitmessage_link: A directory-based answer to the key-distribution problem that Bitmessage avoids by having no directory (addresses encode keys) at the cost of out-of-band address exchange.

title: Hey there! You are using WhatsApp: Enumerating Three Billion Accounts for Security and Privacy
note: Probed over a hundred million phone numbers per hour against WhatsApp contact discovery without effective rate limiting; census of the user base; nearly half of numbers from the 2021 Facebook leak still active; found reuse of X25519 keys across devices and numbers. Shows an identifier-based directory leaks registration status and metadata at planetary scale despite E2EE.
bitmessage_link: Phone-number identifiers make the directory enumerable; Bitmessage's key-derived addresses avoid enumeration but give up discovery.

title: Practical Attacks on a Decentralized Secure Messenger Session
note: Implementation-driven analysis of Session Protocol V1 (1:1 and closed groups): no mutual public-key authentication and no binding to monotonic counters. Three practical attacks by malicious server nodes or insiders: impersonation via public-key substitution, message timestamp forgery, and message dropping/replay. Concerns authentication and ordering; routing metadata properties not the focus.
bitmessage_link: Shows that dropping Signal's ratchet for a stateless long-term-key design reintroduces the authentication gaps of Bitmessage-style static-key schemes.

title: Formal Security Analysis of the Olvid Messenger
note: First formal (Tamarin) analysis of Olvid, an E2EE messenger without phone numbers used by French officials: verifies mutual authentication, session-key secrecy, forward secrecy and replay protection against an active adversary, but shows Olvid is not secure in the eCK model (does not meet properties of Signal-class protocols), uncovers a potential timing leakage and discusses Olvid's anonymity claims. Content/session analysis with a metadata remark; PDF fetch was throttled (HTTP 429) so only the abstract page was read.
bitmessage_link: A deployed messenger built with identifier-free onboarding and its own AKE/CKA, analysed against the Signal benchmark.
